newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy govt overestimating Eurotax income - Credito.
newsitem.headline: Italy govt overestimating Eurotax income - Credito.

text.p: The Italian government's targets for income from the 1997 'Eurotax' aimed at getting Italy into monetary union are overestimated and revenue is unlikely to be more than 10 trillion lire, Credito Italiano said.
Prime Minister Romano Prodi on Tuesday detailed the new Eurotax, which he forecasts will raise 12.5 trillion lire next year.

Some 5.5 trillion is to come from a one-off income tax hike, 3.5 trillion lire from bringing forward tax on employees' severance payments, 2.5 trillion from payment of taxes already due and one trillion from re-negotiating Italy's foreign currency debt.
Credito said in a research note: "The Eurotax rates around 80 percent on the credibility index."

"We judge it difficult that the part of the budget related to swifter collection of some taxes (2.5 trillion) will bring in the amount expected and we believe the government's figures are overestimated and that the additional revenues will not be more than about 10 trillion," the note said.
Regarding swifter tax collection, Credito noted: "A similar measure was already contained in the June mini-budget and it did not achieve the hoped for results in terms of revenue."
On the whole, the bank judged as generally credible the measures adopted as far as they related to income tax.
But as this was a one-off tax increase, in 1998 it would be necessary to cover the subsequent gap in order to keep down the ratio of the budget deficit to gross domestic product.
At that point it would be difficult to avoid intervening more deeply to correct social services spending, Credit said.
The Euro-tax, which forms part of the government's controversial 1997 budget, is designed to help Italy qualify for European economic and monetary union at the start in 1999.
